Summary

The emotions of despair and hopelessness, Khaslana feeling doomed to be the only one without finding love, it never came. Only the opposite. Only lines of hope, where his feelings extended beyond his own and mentioned an indirect source, a second person that has never been brought up before. There were doubts, mainly of Khaslana himself, but it wasn’t that kind of song. No, because once the song was over, Mydei realized right away that it had been a —

“Love song. Khaslana just wrote a love song.”

Cipher sounded just as surprised as he felt.

Mydei learns why he should always think twice before being a hater.

“Do you want to know what the worst part about this song is?”

Cipher groaned. Castorice paid him no mind.

“No, no,” Mydei quickly continues, leaning forward between the driver and passenger seat so he could turn the volume dial down. “Let me say this, it’s actually a good point.”

“How,” Cipher drawls, adding an irritated ‘uh’ sound to the end. “We’ve, no, you’ve been over this before. You don’t like his music because it’s too sad, excuse us for thinking Sir Frown-a-Lot would resonate with it. Can I turn it up now?” That was absurd. Mydei didn’t frown because he was sad, he frowned because there was nothing to smile about. Those were not the same thing.

Castorice raised her hand. “Can I interrupt long enough to say that it’s actually not that sad of a song? It sounds pretty upbeat.”

“They all do,” Cipher agreed, as if that made a difference.

Mydei sat back, shaking his head at the two girls in the front. “I don’t care if he’s singing to the beat of fucking California Girls, he’s still talking about being alone forever as if he’s not a grown man who can just, I don’t know, go outside? Meet some people? Am I missing something here?”

“Sympathy,” Castorice says.

“A sense of enjoyment,” Cipher adds.

Cyrene chimed in. “I think Mydei has a point.”

“Thank you.”

Cipher looked away from the road long enough to shoot a defensive look towards her through the rear view mirror. “What the hell, Rene? Don’t enable him. I thought you liked Khaslana.”

“I do,” the pink haired woman nodded. “He can actually carry a tune, unlike some other people in this car.” She gave Cipher a pointed stare back, her face implying the rest.

Cipher sucked in through her teeth. “Damn. Poor Castorice.”

Cyrene shook her head. “Anyway, I do like his music. Do I think he could have a little more faith in himself? Probably.” Mydei firmly nodded, glad that someone was on the same page as him. He wouldn’t be so critical about it if the man had at least one song that didn’t reek of pessimism. Granted, Khaslana only had eight songs actually put out, but that alone has given him a rise to fame and now he has to be known as the guy that’s sad all the time. What an image, really. “Then again, misery sells. We're in a heartbreak pandemic now, so it’s a good cash grab.”

Castorice frowned. “I’d say his feelings are more than a cash grab.”

“I just didn’t know it was illegal to feel insecure,” Cipher said, her tone dripping with disbelief. “‘Art is expression’ until someone hates their life, I guess.”

“Well, I don’t think he hates his life,” Castorice presumes. “I just think he feels inadequate as far as love, which still is perfectly normal. A lot of people feel that way when they haven’t experienced a groundbreaking relationship.”

“Mydei,” Cipher coughs.

The blonde scoffs. “The argument is losing its point when we have to start talking about my life.” Whatever similarity he had with the singer was immediately canceled out by one unwavering fact; Mydei never openly expressed it. If anything, his friends brought it up more than he did as if not dating somehow offended them. “You know, for two people obsessed with each other, you two sure are acting like this guy is your third.”

“Pretty sure Khaslana is gay,” Cyrene said, eyes on her phone as she scrolled through her social media.

Mydei scowled. “Not the point and even if it was, how would you know that?” Cyrene only shrugged in response.

Cipher snorted. “We’ve hung around you long enough to know what a gay, romantically absent man is like.”

“Why is this about me again?”

Why did he even let them play the music in the car anyway? The whole ‘whoever sits in the passenger seat gets aux’ rule never bothered Mydei initially, it was practically null considering it ended up being Castorice’s every time. It only started to be an issue when they deemed Doom and Gloom’s eight hit wonders to be the perfect mood setter for what he thought was a pretty good day.

Whatever.

Mydei was well aware that their outing was practically finished, they were only ten minutes from Cyrene’s place so it could’ve been worse. They only started playing Khaslana almost two songs ago, so it’s not like he had been subjected to an evening full of a random stranger’s struggles. He just couldn’t understand why two people like Cipher and Castorice could act like they related so much, when the target audience was clearly people just like the singer. Single, sad, any ‘s’ word that was the exact opposite of what the two girls were.

Maybe misery did sell. Maybe other people’s misery really was someone else’s entertainment.

“I think we should talk about something else,” Castorice suggested, turning the radio off completely. He internally thanked her. “What are people saying about the movie, Cyrene?”

The pink haired woman hummed, eyes on her phone. “The usual. ‘This movie changed my life,’ ‘I sobbed the whole time,’ things like that. Glad to know I’m not the only one who cried.”

“Careful,” Cipher warned. “Mydei might complain about the direction of the movie if you talk about how sad it was. We should choose our next words very carefully.”

Mydei couldn’t stop himself from scoffing. “The movie was my idea to begin with.” He was the only one in the group who read the book beforehand too, thank you very much. Misery in a movie did not equate to that in songs, there was depth to the emotions because films were built around unrealistic narratives. There was meaning, and what meaning did Khaslana songs have? That he couldn’t find love in this loveless world? Join the club, dude.

“There’s apparently a lot of fan edits already,” Cyrene said, the sounds of music cutting in and out as she scrolled. “Guess I was right. Sadness does sell.”

Cipher furrowed her brows. “What’s the difference between a lack of relationship in a movie and a lack of relationship in a song? The main character got the shitty end of the stick, Khaslana has about five songs that can thoroughly relate to it. You’re just being nitpicky.”

“Hello?” Mydei questioned, genuinely offended. “The main character was doomed from the beginning, not to mention he has to kill his lover in every lifetime. There was never going to be a happy ending. Khaslana is just being insecure.”

“Mydei you’re literally insecure,” Cipher countered.

Castorice glanced back with concern. “Mydei, are you insecure?”

“He is.”

“I’m not,” he clarified. If it were anyone else, he’d be irritated that he even gave the impression of not feeling secure with himself. He was just well aware of the fact that Cipher’s favorite pastime was getting on his last nerves. “Even if I were, you don’t see me sitting in my room singing about it.”

The grey haired woman mumbled, “god forbid someone has a hobby.” That wasn’t a hobby. That was just sad, and no, Mydei was not being a hater. He happened to think he was just being very critical, even if people liked to think it was too harsh. Someone has to be the one to take initiative, especially when everyone else reveled in that guy’s sorrows. Mydei was not so easily swayed. “You’re, like, the king of projection right now, dude.”

“Explain.”

Castorice sighed. “We really shouldn’t.”

“Think about it,” Cipher said, glancing up through the rear view. “You’re so emotionally repressed that the idea of vocally expressing your feelings gives you this weird look on your — yes, that one. Thank you.” Mydei rolled his eyes. “Maybe you just refuse to let yourself enjoy the music. Maybe the idea of you relating to something would knock some bricks off of that wall of nonchalance and we can’t have that, can we?”

What the hell?

The worst part about it? She was wrong.

Mydei had a secret, one he wouldn’t share with anyone currently in the vehicle no matter how little of a deal it was. Truly, the earth would continue to rotate even if they did know. Cipher may have a slick comment here and there, but nothing would change if they found out the truth. That Mydei did relate to his music. That he had all eight songs saved in a private playlist, completely hidden from the one he allowed his friends to see.

That didn’t mean he was a fan.

He knew why he didn’t tell the others, because explaining to them that saving the songs did not mean liking the artist would completely go over their heads. It was infuriating, if anything. He didn’t ask to resonate so much with a guy who sings about feeling lonely, Mydei was fine forcing his own loneliness aside. In silence. He didn’t understand how Khaslana could be so open about it, as if laying himself bare to all of his listeners would suddenly make his problems go away. Mydei could never do that. How could anyone, really?

Sometimes he considered that Khaslana was being too dramatic.

That, or maybe Khaslana had been the problem all along. Then again, it didn’t make sense considering the man held nothing back in his songs. His lyrics were too see through, as if showing that much vulnerability was no big deal to him. So in a way, Mydei and all of his fans could understand the kind of person he was. The kind of man who cared too deeply yet was scared to give that to others, fearing for the sake of his heart. In every line in every song, one could see that Khaslana was as genuine as they came.

That’s what pissed Mydei off the most.

How could someone like that still get so unlucky? If a person who had no qualms about expressing himself and his intentions could go without finding love, what hope was there for Mydei? A man who was the exact opposite. He could not imagine being so vocal to people he’s never even met, yet he was inclined to the same fate as an artist who did.

So no, he didn’t like Khaslana. Not because of the reasons he liked to spew out, but because the artist had no reason to expose himself so willingly. Mydei saw no reason as to why he would intentionally show his heart to the world when everyone else was the problem. A person like that didn’t deserve for his issues to be treated as a form of entertainment, especially when Khaslana knew that was the case.

Maybe Mydei just didn’t understand it at all.

He wasn’t heartless by any means, however. He was able to admit — to himself — that the singer had a good voice, that partially being the reason Mydei listened to the music as much as he did. It was captivating, as if his tone alone was meant to lure people in and Mydei was one of many victims. The blonde still thought he was using his voice for all the wrong reasons, broadcasting his hurt to people who didn’t even know him.

Then again, Cipher was right. Music is expression, not to mention he’s never held this thought towards anyone until Khaslana.

He didn’t know why.

It didn’t matter, because he wouldn’t try explaining this to his friends. They wouldn’t understand either.

The car only fell silent for a few seconds after Cipher’s words, Mydei too caught up in his own head to retort back. Castorice shot a stern look towards her girlfriend.

“Cipher, that wasn’t nice.”

“Oh my god,” she said with a groan. “I meant it with love, obviously. Mydei, if you being emotionally stunted bothered us then we wouldn’t keep you around.”

He deadpanned. “Thanks.”

“We love you, Deimy,” Cyrene consoled, eyes still glued to her phone. It was hard to appreciate the sentiment. “Oh hey, look at this fan edit.” She turned the device his way, pressing the screen so he could watch.

Mydei rolled his eyes.

Of course it was to a Khaslana song.

Cipher flopped down onto the sofa. “What about ‘Cycles?’”

When Mydei thought arriving at Cyrene's would free him of the music discourse, he should’ve known he was getting too confident in Cipher’s ability to let something go. Or in his case, lack thereof.

“The same as before,” Mydei said with zero interest, already having said his opinion on four other songs. “I still think he’s using a not so slow beat to hide how sad the song actually is.” He totally hasn’t given that one any thought before.

Castorice sat down on the couch beside her girlfriend, picking up Cipher’s sprawled out legs to place them over her lap. “I don’t necessarily think that’s a bad thing, nor do I think he’s trying to hide it. I think anyone listening can appreciate the melody while understanding the perpetual loop of hope and disappointment he’s talking about.”

“You would think Mydei would relate to that,” Cipher muttered while reaching for the remote, already making herself at home. Cyrene hadn’t even made it inside the place yet.

Mydei sat down on the opposite couch. “Of course not. You know what they say about hope and what it breeds.”

“Yeah,” she scoffed. “Maybe the only thing needing to get bred is you so you can quit being so damn pessimistic.”

“But when Khaslana does it, everyone swoons?”

“He has a lovely voice,” Castorice chimed in.

Mydei scowled. “No he doesn’t.” Yes, he really does.

“Khaslana also tries,” the grey haired woman added. “You do what, growl at everyone who tries to talk to you? Then you have the audacity to say you’re not fit for relationships. Like, gee, I wonder who set that system up.” Mydei does not growl at everyone who tries to talk to him. No one tries to talk to him because they assume he will growl. Does it make much of a difference in the end? Probably not, but the least she could do was acknowledge the truth.

He crossed his arms. “I never said not being fit for relationships bothered me.”

Cipher shrugged. “Well it bothers me. How can I ever play the role of a protective best friend if you won’t get that stick out of your ass?”

“I happen to like this stick in my ass.”

Castorice looked up with concern. “Um—”

“Try something else then,” Cipher interjected. “Or someone else. Anything to loosen you up, and yes that pun was intended.”

Mydei rolled his eyes. “You either want me to date or hook up, but you can’t have both.”

“At this rate, I won’t have either if you—”

The sound of a crash down the hall cut her off.

They looked at each other first, then at the front door as if trying to remember whether or not Cyrene managed to make it in the apartment. No, they would’ve seen her. She’s small in build but she’s not that easy to miss. As far as they knew, there was no one else here, Cyrene only planned this movie marathon with the four of them. Mydei could have been wrong then, maybe they really just missed it. Their friend could’ve slipped inside after them and it just went unnoticed.

When the front door opened and Cyrene stepped inside, he realized that was not the case.

“Sorry,” she said, toeing her shoes off. “My mother called.”

“Uh,” Cipher drawled, eyes flickering back and forth between the hallway and their pink haired friend. “Cyrene, don't look now, but I’m pretty sure your place is haunted. As fuck.”

“What?” Cyrene said, following her gaze towards the hall. Just then another loud noise could be heard, though this time it was followed by a muffled voice. She rolled her eyes, shaking her head. “Oh, that’s just my brother being exceptionally loud again. He moved back home a few days ago so I’m giving him the guest room for now. Apparently he’s still in the process of unpacking. Just ignore him.”

Mydei didn’t know much about her brother, just that he spent three years away traveling so he could, according to Cyrene, find himself. With what money? He didn’t know, nor did he bother to ask. His family seemed to be supportive of it nonetheless so it didn’t seem like anything worth questioning. He’s only seen a few pictures of the guy as well, all of which were from the time before his departure and not currently accurate. Mydei doubted a guy could change that much in three years, then again being on the road could’ve taken him down a very unpleasant route. Mentally and physically.

“Phineas?” Cipher asked, relaxing back on the couch once she realized the apartment was not haunted. “Did all of his soul searching not work out for him? That’s a shame. He’s not, like… a crackhead or anything, is he?”

Cyrene smirked, taking a seat beside Mydei. “Phainon, and no.” Another loud sound echoed through the place and she sighed. “Unfortunately he hasn’t grasped the idea of not living alone anymore.”

Worry washed over Castorice. “You don’t need to go check on him, do you?”

“Of course not,” Cyrene waved her off. “I’d be more concerned if he wasn’t making any noise.”

“He can join us for movie night if he wants,” Cipher suggested. Mydei cocked a brow. He didn’t even know the guy, but that alone is why he wasn’t too keen on the idea. Phainon clearly was someone loud, what if he was the type of person to talk the whole time? Or worse, what if he was the type to predict the ending of the movie and completely ruin it for everyone else? Call him soft, but Mydei hated spoilers, and he’d be damned if he let some stranger mess up a movie for him.

Cyrene shrugged. “Maybe. He’s probably going to be too busy writing, or whatever.”

Castorice perked up. “He writes stories as well?”

Loud but intellectual? Mydei would just have to see this for himself.

“Well,” the pink haired woman said, tilting her head as if she was genuinely contemplating the answer regarding her own brother. “Yeah, you could say that.”

“Maybe he would be willing to share?”

Cipher groaned. “Love you big time, Cas, but I only put up with reading when it’s yours. Please don’t put me through this.” Castorice gave her a firm look, a silent scold with her eyes.

Cyrene just laughed. “Don’t worry, I don’t think he’s the sharing type anyways.”

“Then I like him already,” Cipher said. What a disappointment. Unlike his friend, Mydei would have been willing to read whatever it was the man wrote. Based on the fact that he likely wouldn’t share probably meant it was something more personal, stories and feelings most likely pertaining to his time on the road. A diary if he really wanted to get technical, but he supposed that wasn’t outside the realm of normal. People wrote down what they felt all the time.

Some a little too much.

This wasn’t about Khaslana right now, though.

“Must feel weird seeing him after so long,” Castorice thought. “You haven’t seen him since your freshman year.” They only met Cyrene during their sophomore year of college, so the three of them didn’t have the chance to meet Phainon before he left. She hardly mentioned her brother, though topics never came up where it was suitable enough for discussion.

Cyrene huffed in amusement. “Honestly, it doesn’t feel weird at all. We talked pretty much all the time.”

“How old is he again?” Cipher asked. “Thirty?”

Cyrene frowned. “He just turned twenty-five.” That wasn’t much older than them, they had all hit twenty-two already being in their last year of school. “Still acts like a child sometimes. I had to boil his water the other night.”

Cipher slowly tore her gaze away from the TV. “Did he ask you to?”

“Nope,” the pink haired woman answered, popping the ‘p.’ “He burnt himself on the stove before he could actually boil the water. Figured I’d save him from potentially melting his skin off.” Mydei didn’t like to form an impression on people he has yet to meet, but he could very well figure out that Phainon was not like his sister. The privacy in what he did was one thing, Cyrene was an open book. Not knowing how to boil water? Even someone as clumsy as Cipher could do that.

None of them had the chance to respond when they heard the sound of footsteps from the hallway, all eyes in the room landing on where the man would soon appear.

It hit Mydei like whiplash when he did.

Truth was, he has never been separated long enough with someone to witness a change made in a few years. Everyone he ever knew has been in his life since the moment he’s met them, so it was only natural for him to think Phainon couldn’t have changed that much from the few pictures he’s seen. If his memory served him correctly, the guy had been tall and lanky, his features making him look younger than he actually had been. Mydei recalled seeing braces too, giving him a genuine dorky — he was being real, not rude — vibe.

This?

This was not a dorky vibe.

Standing in front of them now was nothing but broad shoulders and muscle. His blank tank top fit snugly against his chest, doing little to hide the six — maybe eight — pack of abs underneath. Grey sweatpants covered the length of thick thighs all the way down to his sock clad feet, and Mydei realized now that he was probably staring too much at the guy's body but he didn’t care. Phainon wasn’t even looking at him, so he could get away with it. Once his eyes finally made its way to his head, the baby face was no longer evident as it showed something more refined. Aged. Literally everything that could make a man or woman swoon.

Not that Mydei was swooning, of course.

The one thing that remained the same was the hair. Fluffy, white locks sat messily atop his head, somehow suiting him even more. He was almost like a puppy, though calling him that felt rather unfitting. Dog seemed like the proper word, because this man…

Yeah, maybe three years could change a lot.

It was good to see the road did him good, causing him to grow in a way more suitable for his age and not in a way that made him look older. It was pretty much a miracle.

“Oh,” Phainon said once he noticed everyone’s presence, looking as if he were a deer caught in headlights. “I didn’t know you had company, Rene.”

She raised a brow. “I told you this morning what my plans were.”

He scratched the back of his neck. “Did you? Oh, hey—” He then began to look around, eyes lingering on Mydei the longest before he continued. “This must be the infamous C3 and Mydeimos I’ve heard so much about.”

Mydei’s mouth moved before he could stop it. “Mydei. Only the people close to me get to call me Mydeimos.” This caused blue eyes to widen, probably not expecting an answer so blunt. Mydei wasn’t going to take it back, though.

“Man, there’s really no hope for you,” Cipher muttered under her breath.

"Mydei then,” Phainon corrected, his caught off expression morphing into a smile. Of course the braces were gone as well, accentuating straight, white teeth that were practically perfect. “Rene mentioned you were a tougher nut to crack.”

Excuse him? Mydei was a perfectly reasonable nut to crack, he just didn’t let everyone he met crack him. His real name was a personal thing anyway, not giving Cyrene’s brother — a total stranger — the luxury of using it did not automatically paint him as reserved. Was he? Cipher liked to think so, and even Mydei knew he wasn’t the most outgoing person, but he still—

Wait a second.

The blonde turned to Cyrene. “You mentioned me?”

She knitted her brows, unaware of what the issue was. “Yeah? I mentioned all of you. Are you guys not staples in my life?” Well that was sweet, but it didn’t take away from Mydei’s confusion. What else was there to say about him to her brother, besides the crazy line of being a ‘tough nut to crack.’ Seriously, who even says that anymore?

“Oh!” Cipher sat up abruptly, legs still laid across her girlfriend’s lap. “What did she say about me? Tell me, tell me.”

Phainon laughed. “Cipher right?” She nodded. “Hm. A bit insane…” That was true. “A little unhinged.” A little? Not what Mydei would say. “Quite the trickster. Oh, also the nutcracker to this one.” He had the audacity to point at Mydei.

The grey haired woman sighed. “I try. Unfortunately Mydei doesn’t let anyone crack him.”

The blonde scowled. “What the fuck?” Yes it was the exact same way he described it, but did she have to word it like that out loud? Why was Phainon so obsessed with his introverted nature in the first place? It was a shame too, Mydei thought he was a rather pleasant sight until he went and opened his mouth. “Not everyone has to be a showboat. Castorice is quieter than me.”

Cipher rolled her eyes. “Castorice isn’t mean.”

“How the fuck am I mean?” He didn’t get an answer, looking around to see everyone purposely avoiding doing so. Even Phainon had the nerve to look away, a shit-eating grin on his face as if he found the whole thing ironic. Whatever. Mydei wasn’t dealing with this right now. “All of you can kiss my ass.”

Phainon laughed, loud and obxionous and definitely not music to Mydei’s ears. “If I do, will that finally earn me the right to call you Mydeimos?”

“No.”

“Can’t say I didn’t try,” the man shrugged. “Anyways, I came down to borrow the TV but since you guys are here, I can make myself scarce.”

Mydei didn’t spare him a glance. “Thank y—”

“You should join us,” Cipher interjected, shooting a quick and teasing smirk Mydei’s way. Proving once again she could be the bane of his existence if she really wanted to.

“Are you sure?” Phainon asked, caught off guard once more. “I don’t want to intrude if this is some bonding experience for you guys. I shouldn’t be involved until I’m allowed to call Mydei by his real name.” Mydei rolled his eyes.

Cipher waved him off. “Please, you wouldn’t be intruding at all. We’re just binging the Zagreus movies.”

Phainon’s brows raised at that. “Oh hey, I loved those movies. I still can’t get over everyone only staying alive because of Zagreus’ lie.” Amber eyes widened once the words left Phainon’s mouth, Mydei’s head slowly turning to face him. His dumb smile did nothing but irk the blonde in that moment and Cipher immediately noticed the change in her friend’s demeanor, bursting out into a fit of laughter. Phainon looked around in confusion. “What? Are we not talking about the same movies?”

“Oh boy,” Castorice said quietly.

Cyrene shook her head. “Mydei’s never seen the movies.” This only caused Cipher to laugh even harder. Mydei couldn’t even be surprised, it was the exact reason he didn’t want the guy joining them for movie night to begin with. He just really hated being spoiled, if that wasn’t already clear, and would’ve much rather preferred for Phainon to be a talker instead of what every movie watcher despised.

The white haired male gasped. “I… am so sorry.” Mydei didn’t care. He continued to glare at him and if looks could kill, Phainon would’ve dropped to the ground already. “Okay, but in my defense, the movies have been finished for six years. Surely that wasn’t the first spoiler you’ve heard.”

“Phainon dude,” Cipher said between laughter. “You’re a treat.”

Mydei scoffed. “A bitter one.”

“Treats can’t be bitter,” Phainon teased.

Mydei gave a dry smile. “First time for everything.”

Cipher threw her legs off of Castorice’s lap, standing from the couch. “Look, Mydei, just pretend you didn’t hear the shit Phainon said. We’re not going to spend the entire night deciding on movies because of your fussy taste.” She then made her way to the kitchen, not even giving him a chance to respond. Rude. Mydei wasn’t going to change his mind anyway, especially because of Cyrene’s brother. He just has to hope Phainon had half the mind not to spoil anything else.

“We can watch something else,” Castorice offered.

The blonde shook his head. “Don’t worry about it. Loud mouth over here would ruin the ending of that too.”

“Please cut me some slack,” Phainon pleaded while pushing off of the wall he leaned on, sitting on the couch with Cyrene between him and Mydei. “How was I supposed to know you’re not up to date with hit movies? Pretty, pretty please forgive me?”

“Grown ass man,” Mydei mumbled.

Now that he has actually met the man, he finally had the chance to form an opinion on Phainon yet nothing came to mind. Yeah, he was insanely attractive, pretty much rendering Mydei speechless initially, but that wasn’t all. It didn’t take away from his stubborn personality, pushing Mydei’s buttons and knowing he was doing so. This was their first time speaking to each other, how could it have been that easy for him to match even Cipher’s level?

A few moments passed and Cyrene stood up as well. “She’s been in there for a while, I’m going to go help her find a snack.
